extracted.intended_audience: taxpayers, tax professionals (accountants/attorneys), employers, and public commenters on IRS proposed regulations
extracted.subtask_description: Proposed Treasury/IRS regulations defining and limiting the deduction for 'qualified tips' under section 224, including definitions (cash tips, voluntariness), dollar limits and phaseouts, exclusions (illegal activity, SSTBs), reporting rules, and occupational-list mapping. Intended to guide taxpayers' eligibility and reporting and to solicit public comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deduction allowed for qualified tips reported on specified forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Under section 224(a) there is allowed a deduction under section 63(b) equal to the qualified tips received by an individual during the taxable year that are included separately on statements furnished to the individual pursuant to section 6041(d)(3), section 6041A(e)(3), section 6050W(f)(2), or section 6051(a)(18) of the Code, or reported by the taxpayer on Form 4137 (or successor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qualified tips must be included separately on the enumerated statements (e.g., W-2) or reported on Form 4137 (or successor). The preamble also references that Form 1099-NEC, Form 1099-K, and Form 1099-MISC may be used to report tips for purposes of the deduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annual deduction dollar limit
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount allowed as a deduction for any taxable year shall not exceed $25,000, regardless of filing status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This $25,000 cap applies before applying the modified adjusted gross income phaseout described in paragraph (b)(2). Examples in the regulation illustrate application of the $25,000 cap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phaseout based on modified adjusted gross income
rubrics_metrics.description: After applying the $25,000 limitation, the allowable deduction is further reduced (but not below zero) by $100 for each $1,000 by which the taxpayer's modified adjusted gross income exceeds $150,000 ($300,000 for a joint return).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For purposes of paragraph (b)(2), 'modified adjusted gross income' means adjusted gross income increased by amounts excluded under sections 911, 931, or 933. The regulation gives numeric examples showing dividing the excess by $1,000 and multiplying by $100 to compute the reduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualified tips — occupation requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject to other requirements, 'qualified tips' are amounts received as cash tips by an individual in an occupation that customarily and regularly received tips on or before December 31, 2024, as provided in paragraph (f) of the section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eligibility depends on whether the individual's occupation appears on the Treasury 'List of Occupations that Receive Tips' (paragraph (f)). The preamble explains the list provides clarity so similar taxpayers receive consistent tax treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cash tips — permitted forms
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of qualified tips, 'cash tips' are tips received from customers or, in the case of an employee, through a mandatory or voluntary tip-sharing arrangement (such as a tip pool), that are paid in a cash medium of exchange, including cash, check, credit card, debit card, gift card, tangible or intangible tokens readily exchangeable for a fixed amount in cash (such as casino chips), and any other form of electronic settlement or mobile payment application denominated in cash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cash tips do not include items paid in any medium other than cash (e.g., event tickets, meals, services, or most digital assets). For these purposes, a 'tip' is an amount paid by customers for services that is in excess of the amount agreed to, required, charged, or otherwise reasonably expected to have to be paid for the services in an arm's-length transaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntariness requirement (no compulsion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Amounts are qualified tips only if they are paid voluntarily and without any consequence in the event of nonpayment, are not the subject of negotiation, and are determined by the payor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule means service charges, automatic gratuities, and other mandatory amounts automatically added to a bill are not qualified tips even if distributed to employees. If a customer is expressly provided an option to disregard or modify amounts added to a bill, those amounts are not mandatory (and may be qualified if paid voluntarily). The regulation provides multiple illustrative examples (POS device options, recommended tips with a modify option, party-of-six automatic charges vs separate voluntary additions) to show how voluntariness is applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service charges and automatic gratuities excluded
rubrics_metrics.description: Service charges, automatic gratuities, and any other mandatory amounts automatically added to a customer's bill by the vendor or establishment are not qualified tips.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if such mandatory charges are subsequently distributed to employees, they are not qualified tips for the section 224 deduction. The preamble examples include an automatic 18% charge added without customer ability to modify or disregard (not qualified).

rubrics_metrics.name: POS/checkout forced-tip selection rules
rubrics_metrics.description: If a POS device forces a customer to select a tip amount greater than zero (no option to leave no tip), the lowest required portion is not a qualified tip; any amount the customer voluntarily adds above that required amount may be a qualified tip.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a POS with options including 'no tip' — selection of 18% is qualified; a POS that requires selecting 15%/18%/20% with no 'no tip' option — the minimum forced amount (15%) is not qualified, but any amount above that that the customer voluntarily pays is qualified (e.g., selecting 18% means 3% above the required 15% is qualified).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contractual pre-agreed gratuities and reclassified charges not qualified
rubrics_metrics.description: Amounts that are included in a service contract or agreed price (e.g., a gratuity included in the contract before services) are not qualified tips; amounts reclassified by the service provider from the agreed contract price are not qualified tips but are part of the charge for services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: a 15% 'service charge' included in a painting contract is not a qualified tip; an extra cash payment after service completion that the payor designates as a tip may be qualified. If a payer pays more than the agreed amount and the provider records part as a tip but that excess was effectively part of the charge, only the portion actually determined by the payor as a tip is qualified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specified service trade or business (SSTB) exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: An amount received by an individual in the course of a specified service trade or business (as defined in section 199A(d)(2)) is not a qualified tip. If an individual performs services as an employee, the relevant trade or business is the employer's trade or business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples clarify that a self-employed performer in the performing arts (an SSTB) cannot treat tips received in that trade as qualified tips. Conversely, an employee pianist working for a hotel that is not an SSTB may have qualified tips despite performing services in an occupational field that is an SSTB, because the employer's trade or business is not an SSTB. The rule focuses on the employer's trade or business when services are performed as an employee.

rubrics_metrics.name: TRDA/GITCA tip-rate reporting rules for employees
rubrics_metrics.description: Employees who enter into a Tipped Employee Participation Agreement (TRDA) or a Model Gaming Employee Tip Reporting Agreement (GITCA) may determine the amount of their qualified tips using the applicable tip rates in their agreement (as reported on Form W-2) or amounts reported on Form 4137.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of TRDA/GITCA to determine qualified tips does not affect tip audit protection. Employees under such agreements may still report the full amount of their tips in excess of the established tip rate on Form 4137 (or to their employer) and use that full reported amount as qualified tips for the deduction. The regulation includes a gambling dealer example where the W-2 reports the tip-rate amount and employees may claim that reported amount as qualified tips if other section 224 requirements are met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tips received while performing illegal services excluded
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualified tips do not include tips that were received while performing a service that is a felony or misdemeanor under applicable law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: tips received while performing services in human trafficking, exotic pet smuggling, counterfeiting or fencing stolen goods, drug trafficking, drug dealing, and unlicensed sales that violate applicable law are not eligible for the deduction. The preamble explains the exclusion clarifies that tips earned while violating applicable law are not 'qualified tips.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Occupation mapping methodology and limitations for the TTOC/SOC list
rubrics_metrics.description: Occupation codes are matched to SOC codes and related to Treasury Tipped Occupation Codes (TTOC) using the self-reported character strings in the 'Your occupation' box on Form 1040; mismatches and self-reports that do not correspond to W-2 occupations can prevent matching to a TTOC code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble notes data shortcomings (e.g., taxpayers entering 'Student' instead of 'bartender' or misspellings) as primary reasons the percentage of all reported tips mapped to occupations in the table sums to only 67.4%. The mapping approach and limitations are explained to provide context for the List of Occupations that Receive Tips and invite comments on classification issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reported tips statistical threshold ($100)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the statistics used to create the occupational table, 'reported tips' are defined as at least $100 of tips reported on a W-2 or Form 4137.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes to Table A explain that the percentage of individuals within related SOC codes who have at least $100 of tips reported are counted; an asterisk indicates a share of less than 0.1% or a small cell size. This threshold is used for the empirical analysis underpinning the occupation list.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms and reporting mechanisms that can support qualified-tip claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualified-tip amounts may be those included separately on statements (e.g., W-2) or reported on Form 4137 (or successor); the preamble also references Form 1099-NEC, Form 1099-K, and Form 1099-MISC as reporting vehicles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regulation explicitly ties qualified tips to amounts reported to the IRS via the enumerated Code-authorized statements or reported on Form 4137, meaning proper reporting on those forms is a prerequisite to claiming the deduction. The TRDA/GITCA programs and reporting via tip pools are addressed as part of acceptable reporting methods when consistent with program terms.
